name: Hittite Empire
summary: An Anatolian empire that rivalled Egypt. It fought the Battle of Kadesh and signed one of the earliest known peace treaties.

location.value: Central Anatolia (modern Turkey), ruled from Hattusa.

terrain.value: A high plateau with mountains and the Kızılırmak (Halys) river.
terrain.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

climate.value: Drought and famine are mentioned in the late 13th century BCE.
climate.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

resources.value: Metals (copper, silver, iron), timber and grain.
resources.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

disasters.value: Famine and drought at the end of the Bronze Age (late 13th century BCE).
disasters.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

population.value: Estimates range from about 140,000 to over 200,000.

urbanisation.value: Hattusa was a large walled city with temples and palaces.
urbanisation.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

disease.value: A plague raged for about 20 years under Mursili II, reportedly brought by Egyptian prisoners.
disease.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

migration.value: Sea Peoples and Phrygians moved into the region at the end of the empire.
migration.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

economicBase.value: A barter economy based on farming, herding and metals.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Assyria, Egypt, Mycenae and Syria.
tradeRoutes.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

moneyAndTax.value: Barter; gold, copper, silver and bronze measured in shekels and minas.

inequality.value: King and nobles at the top; farmers and dependent labour below.
inequality.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

governmentType.value: Monarchy. The king was ruler, judge and high priest.

keyRulers.value: Labarna I, Mursili I, Šuppiluliuma I (mid-14th century BCE), Muwatalli II, Hattusili III, Šuppiluliuma II (last).

succession.value: Hereditary; the Edict of Telipinu (c. 1525 BCE) set rules of succession after years of murders.
succession.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

institutions.value: Written laws (the Hittite law code) and treaties with vassal kings.

stability.value: Frequent succession crises in the Old Kingdom.
stability.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

eliteConflict.value: Hattusili III seized the throne from his nephew.
eliteConflict.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

armyAndTech.value: Successful use of chariots carrying three men.

majorWars.value: Battle of Kadesh against Egypt (c. 1274 BCE); sack of Babylon (c. 1595 BCE).

territoryChange.value: At its peak it ruled most of Anatolia and northern Syria.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Egypt, Assyria, Mitanni. A peace treaty with Egypt (c. 1259 BCE).

inventions.value: Early ironworking is often attributed to the Hittites, but this is increasingly contested.

scienceEducation.value: Scribes kept archives of clay tablets in several languages.
scienceEducation.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

openness.value: Adopted Hurrian, Mesopotamian and Luwian culture; a “thousand gods”.
openness.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

religion.value: Hittite religion, with storm gods (Tarhunt) as chief deities.

languageWriting.value: Hittite, Luwian, Hattic and Hurrian; Hittite and Luwian are the oldest attested Indo-European languages.

artsArchitecture.value: The Lion Gate at Hattusa and the rock sanctuary of Yazılıkaya.
artsArchitecture.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

socialStructure.value: King, nobles, free people, and dependent people.
socialStructure.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king, who served the storm god as his chief priest.
sharedIdentity.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

neighbours.value: Egypt, Assyria, Mitanni, Babylon, Arzawa and Mycenaean Greeks (Ahhiyawa).

ideasReligions.value: Hittite traditions continued in the Neo-Hittite city-states of Syria.
ideasReligions.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

colonisation.value: Ruled vassal kingdoms in Syria and Anatolia through written treaties.
colonisation.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

riseSignals.value: Unification of Anatolian cities; capital at Hattusa.

peakPeriod.value: Under Šuppiluliuma I (mid-14th century BCE), when the Hittites defeated Mitanni and controlled Syria.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Hittites (checked 6 Nov 2026); Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

declineSignals.value: Famine, attacks by the Kaska and Sea Peoples, and pressure from Assyria.
declineSignals.source: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2005)

outcome.value: Collapse around 1190 BCE; Hattusa was destroyed. Successors: Neo-Hittite states.

sources.value: Clay tablets from Hattusa, deciphered by Hrozný (1915). Checked against Wikipedia (“Hittites”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Bronze Age dates vary between chronologies.

knownFor.label: Three-man war chariots
knownFor.note: Heavy chariots used at the Battle of Kadesh.

knownFor.label: Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty
knownFor.note: One of the earliest surviving peace treaties.

knownFor.label: Lion Gate of Hattusa
knownFor.note: A gateway of carved stone lions in the capital’s walls.
